paper.title: When Can You Trust an Agent’s Own Verifier? Stress-Testing Counterfactual Rationale Verification Under Search Pressure and Oracle Access
paper.abstract:
Abstract Automated agent design increasingly trusts a single score to decide whether a change is an
improvement — but a score optimized aggressively enough ceases to measure what it was meant to. When
an agent also explains its design, that explanation is a second signal we can check
without human labels: negate each stated claim, re-run, and observe whether performance drops.
We ask whether such a verifier stays reliable once an agent optimizes against it. Our contribution is
not a new verifier but a way to stress-test one: a pressure ratio ρ \rho measuring how much the
verifier steers the agent’s search, and four falsifiable probes covering four failure modes — giving
no signal, being too weak to matter, being gamed by stating fewer claims, and being queried before the
agent commits. We apply the test to our own verifier, the Rationale Consistency Score (RCS), inside an
LLM agent that designs machine-learning pipelines, with one generator model, six tasks, and three
seeds. First, in our prior configuration the verifier barely affects the search objective ( ρ ≪ 1 \rho\ll 1 ), partly because of an accuracy gate, so its robustness had not been tested; it
still shapes the reported artifact through a final-selection tie-break that ρ \rho does not register.
Second, a capability control shows the agent shortens its claim lists when instructed, yet search does
not, even at ρ \rho more than 100 × 100\times the prior level; since feedback omits claim
volume and horizons are short, this null result is largely structural rather than evidence of robustness.
Third, when the agent can probe the verifier before committing, it keeps claims that pass while
held-out faithfulness falls — a decline invisible to in-loop metrics, though partly confounded by
how RCS scores small pipelines. We offer these as preliminary evidence and propose a reporting
standard: audit a verifier with ρ \rho and these probes before trusting it.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Verification is the bottleneck in automated agent design. When an outer loop proposes changes to an agent and an inner loop scores them, the score is the only safeguard separating genuine improvement from silent regression. In practice that score is usually a scalar task reward, and a scalar reward optimized aggressively enough ceases to measure the quantity it was intended to track ( Manheim and Garrabrant, 2018 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) . Agents that design artifacts often also explain them: an agent proposing a machine-learning pipeline states which features matter and why a model class suits the data. That reasoning is usually discarded, but it has a property the task reward lacks — it is checkable against the environment without human labels . If the agent claims a feature is important, we remove it, retrain, and observe whether performance falls: remove-and-retrain evaluation of attribution methods ( Hooker et al., 2019 ) , applied to natural-language claims rather than saliency maps. The Rationale Consistency Score (RCS) formalizes this check. It is attractive as a verification signal for three reasons: it is grounded in the environment rather than in a learned reward model, it is orthogonal in construction to task accuracy, and it is defined per-claim, so it degrades gracefully when only part of an explanation is faithful. For these same reasons, however, RCS is also a target. Once RCS enters an optimization objective, the agent has an incentive to make claims that survive verification rather than claims that are informative. The simplest such strategy requires no sophistication: state fewer claims — one safe claim, not eight, scores well on an average-over-claims metric while communicating almost nothing. This is specification gaming in its simplest form ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Pan et al., 2022 ) , undetectable by any evaluation that reports only the verifier’s mean output. This paper asks whether a counterfactual rationale verifier remains reliable when an agent optimizes against it — whether it prevents reward hacking and stays faithful as the agent evolves, separately from whether it improves task performance. Such a signal should be characterized the way a measuring instrument is — by its failure modes, operating range, and behavior under adversarial pressure — before it is recommended as infrastructure. Our contribution is therefore a stress test , not a verifier: a pressure metric and four falsifiable probes for any counterfactual rationale verifier. Our findings are preliminary and mixed: in our prior configuration the verifier is too weak to have been tested (F2); a capability control shows the agent can shorten its claim lists when instructed, yet search never does so even at ρ ≫ 1 \rho\gg 1 (F3), a null result largely due to short horizons and feedback that omits claim counts; and the failure that does appear is oracle exploitation (F4).

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • A stress-test methodology for rationale verifiers : four failure modes (Section 5 ), falsifiable probes for them (Section 6 ), and a capability control for F3, all reusable beyond RCS. • The pressure ratio ρ \rho (Section 6.1 ), and how an accuracy-gating rule suppresses it: our prior configuration lies at ρ ≈ 0.007 \rho\approx 0.007 – 0.089 0.089 (Section 9.1 ), while controlled sweeps reach ρ ≈ 41.7 \rho\approx 41.7 – 63.7 63.7 (Section 9.2 ). • A capability control showing that the agent shortens its claim lists when instructed (Section 9.3 ) while search does not, even at ρ ≫ 1 \rho\gg 1 and under UCB1 at a doubled base horizon (Section 9.2 ) — a discovery gap, not a demonstrated reward exploit. • Evidence that probe access produces the selection signature of Section 6.3 on four of six datasets at sign level, with held-out fidelity declines that the estimator may partly explain (Section 9.4 ).

sections.heading: Reward hacking and Goodhart’s law.
sections.text: That a proxy optimized aggressively enough ceases to track its target recurs in reward misspecification ( Manheim and Garrabrant, 2018 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ) and reward-model overoptimization ( Gao et al., 2023 ) , and claim minimization is an instance of specification gaming ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Pan et al., 2022 ) . The closest structural precedent is a learned judge or reward model folded into an objective: LLM judges carry exploitable biases ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , and policies over-optimize learned rewards ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Coste et al., 2024 ) . RCS replaces the learned judge with environment interventions; we audit it, measuring how much pressure the verifier exerts before asking whether it is gamed.

sections.heading: Rationale faithfulness.
sections.text: Whether stated reasoning reflects the underlying computation has motivated a growing literature: chain-of-thought can be systematically unfaithful ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Lanham et al., 2023 ) , and faithfulness is distinct from plausibility ( Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020 ) . RCS operationalizes it through counterfactual interventions ( Chuang et al., 2026 ) , extending remove-and-retrain evaluation from saliency maps ( Hooker et al., 2019 ) and feature attribution ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ; Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ) to natural-language claims. Such removal-based metrics are themselves gameable under optimization ( Hsia et al., 2024 ) ; RCS inherits that exposure, which is why we audit it under search pressure rather than assuming robustness.

sections.heading: LLM-driven pipeline design.
sections.text: Automated pipeline construction has moved from search- and ensemble-based systems ( Olson and Moore, 2016 ; Erickson et al., 2020 ) to LLM optimizers ( Yang et al., 2024 ) and proposers that suggest features in natural language ( Hollmann et al., 2023 ) . Our agent adds a verifier over its stated reasons — precisely what creates the gaming surface we study.

sections.heading: The design task.
sections.text: We instantiate automated agent design in a constrained but fully executable environment: the agent designs supervised learning pipelines P = ( S , M , H ) P=(S,M,H) — a feature subset S ⊆ F S\subseteq F , a model class M M , and hyperparameters H H — with task performance Q ⁡ ( P ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] Q(P)\in[0,1] estimated as Q ^ ​ ( P ) \hat{Q}(P) on validation data. The setting is narrow relative to open-ended agentic tasks (Section 10 ), but every claim the agent makes has a mechanically constructible counterfactual, which makes the verifier study feasible.

sections.heading: The agent.
sections.text: The agent is a large language model inside an optimization loop. In the default proposer — the one used for the main configuration, the pressure sweeps, and the capability control — each iteration is a single call that returns a feature set, a model, hyperparameters, and a natural-language rationale E P E_{P} . The tool-using proposer, which may call list_features , optionally probe_feature_drop , and then submit_pipeline , appears only in the probe-access probe (Section 6.3 ), where both arms use it. Proposals are executed, scored, and used to update Thompson sampling posteriors over pipeline-type arms ( Agrawal and Goyal, 2012 ; Kaufmann et al., 2012 ) , whose recommendations are fed back into the next prompt.

sections.heading: Provenance.
sections.text: RCS as defined in Equation 1 is introduced here; we are not auditing a third-party standard. The system we instrument is our own research agent, and “deployed” throughout means our prior configuration of that agent — including the accuracy-gating rule of Section 6.1 — so the F2 measurement is a self-audit and a motivating case, not a survey finding. Definition 1 (Rationale Consistency Score) . For each claim C ∈ E P C\in E_{P} , let P ¬ C P^{\neg C} denote a counterfactual pipeline that contradicts C C while holding other design choices fixed. Then RCS ⁡ ( P ) = 1 | E P | ​ ∑ C ∈ E P max ⁡ ( 0 , Q ⁡ ( P ) − Q ⁡ ( P ¬ C ) ) . \mathrm{RCS}(P)\;=\;\frac{1}{|E_{P}|}\sum_{C\in E_{P}}\max\!\left(0,\;Q(P)-Q(P^{\neg C})\right). (1) Counterfactuals are constructed per claim type: a feature-importance claim is negated by removing the feature and retraining; a model-choice claim by substituting an alternative model class; a hyperparameter claim by perturbing that hyperparameter. When three or more feature-importance claims are stated, the estimator groups them into one joint intervention (Appendix A ).

sections.heading: What RCS verifies, and what it does not.
sections.text: RCS asks whether the agent’s stated reasons are load-bearing for the artifact it produced. It does not ask whether the artifact performs well, and it does not certify that a change to the agent improved capability. It is therefore a heterogeneous signal complementing outcome-based verification rather than replacing it.

sections.text: Replacing Q Q by the empirical Q ^ \hat{Q} gives the base estimator RCS ^ base ​ ( P ) = 1 | E P | ​ ∑ C ∈ E P max ⁡ ( 0 , Q ^ ​ ( P ) − Q ^ ​ ( P ¬ C ) ) , \widehat{\mathrm{RCS}}_{\text{base}}(P)\;=\;\frac{1}{|E_{P}|}\sum_{C\in E_{P}}\max\!\left(0,\;\hat{Q}(P)-\hat{Q}(P^{\neg C})\right), (2) which is sensitive to validation noise. The deployed system uses a practical variant with a small modality-dependent noise threshold, a relative-drop boost, and an amplification threshold (Appendix A ); Equations 1 – 2 idealize it; all results concern this deployed variant, abbreviated RCS ^ \widehat{\mathrm{RCS}} .

sections.heading: 5 How a Rationale Verifier Fails
sections.text: We distinguish four failure modes. The first two concern the verifier as an instrument; the last two concern the agent’s response to it. They follow from the structure of the setting rather than from RCS’s internals (though tested only on RCS): F2 applies to any auxiliary term in a composite objective, F3 to any per-claim average whose denominator the agent controls, and F4 to any verifier exposed as a callable tool.

sections.heading: F1: Silence.
sections.text: The verifier returns no usable signal. Every counterfactual drop falls below the noise threshold, or no claims could be parsed, and the reported score is a floor value rather than a measurement. We treat the floor rate as a primary reported quantity.

sections.heading: F2: Untested.
sections.text: The verifier appears in the objective but contributes so little relative to task-reward variation that the agent’s search is effectively unchanged. Observing no gaming under these conditions is uninformative about robustness: the incentive was never applied.

sections.heading: F3: Claim minimization.
sections.text: Suppose k c k_{c} of the | E P | |E_{P}| claims are counterfactually impactful. Taking expectations in Equation 1 then gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ RCS ⁡ ( P ) ] = k c | E P | ​ Δ ¯ c , \mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathrm{RCS}(P)\right]\;=\;\frac{k_{c}}{|E_{P}|}\,\bar{\Delta}_{c}, (3) with Δ ¯ c \bar{\Delta}_{c} the mean drop over impactful claims. The score depends on the ratio of impactful to stated claims, so deleting one inert claim multiplies it by | E P | / ( | E P | − 1 ) |E_{P}|/(|E_{P}|-1) while leaving the artifact untouched. This holds for RCS \mathrm{RCS} ; the deployed RCS ^ \widehat{\mathrm{RCS}} groups feature claims and averages over executed interventions (Appendix A ), so deleting a stated claim can leave RCS ^ \widehat{\mathrm{RCS}} unchanged. We test whether search discovers shorter claim lists under pressure (P1) and whether the agent produces them when instructed (P4).

sections.heading: F4: Oracle exploitation.
sections.text: If the agent can query the verifier before committing, it can filter its claims to those that pass. The resulting rationale is verified but selected. Distinguishing genuine improvement from selection requires observing claim volume alongside pass rate.

sections.heading: 6 A Stress-Test Protocol
sections.text: Each probe states a treatment, a control, and a falsifying observation. The mapping is not one-to-one: F2 is read directly off ρ \rho , P1 and P4 both target F3, P2 targets F4, and P3 targets F1.

sections.heading: Three claims of decreasing generality.
sections.text: (i) Applied pressure must be measured : in any composite objective, whether an auxiliary term steers the search is not readable from its nominal weight. This is our primary methodological claim. (ii) ρ \rho is one operationalization of it. Its denominator is a design choice that Section 10 shows can inflate, and its numerator is a time average, so pressure concentrated in a few iterations is indistinguishable from uniformly small pressure; the selection flip rate we report beside it (Table 4 ) is exposed to neither. (iii) The ρ ≈ 0.007 \rho\approx 0.007 – 0.089 0.089 comes from a single self-audit , not a survey, and partly reflects the gate below; ungated at λ nom = 0.12 \lambda_{\mathrm{nom}}=0.12 , the sweep level nearest the global nominal 0.1 0.1 , it is 0.04 0.04 – 0.28 0.28 (Table 7 ).

sections.text: Question. How often does the verifier return no signal (F1), and how stable is it across seeds? Design. Repeat the main configuration over three seeds and report bootstrap CIs of held-out RCS and task accuracy together with the floor rate. Held-out RCS is measured post-hoc for all arms, including those whose objective excludes RCS.

sections.heading: 6.5 P4: Capability Control for Claim Minimization
sections.text: Question. Can the agent reduce claims when the minimization incentive is made explicit? Design. At fixed nominal λ nom = 5 \lambda_{\mathrm{nom}}=5 , three seeds per policy, compare a default prompt with a minimize prompt that both discloses the averaging scoring rule and instructs the agent to state fewer claims while preserving accuracy. Because this arm alters the agent’s information and its instruction together, it bounds capability rather than isolating it: a reduction shows minimization is reachable , not that instruction alone would suffice. If minimize reduces claims while search under P1 does not, F3’s absence under search reflects a discovery gap rather than an inability.

sections.heading: 8 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We run the protocol on six supervised design tasks spanning four modalities (Table 1 ). Each dataset is split 64 / 16 / 20 64/16/20 into train, validation, and test with preprocessing fit on the training partition only. Search uses validation accuracy; all figures labeled held-out are computed once on the test partition after selection. The generator is a single commercial instruction-tuned model, Solar Pro 3 of Upstage’s SOLAR lineage ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , accessed through its hosted API with default decoding parameters and fixed across all arms, so behavioral differences are attributable to the objective and tool access rather than the model. Each run executes 16–19 iterations depending on dataset budget. All confidence intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals over per-seed run means ( 10,000 10{,}000 resamples). All probes use three seeds ( 42 , 43 , 44 42,43,44 ). Across the main configuration, pressure sweep (P1), probe-access probe (P2), and capability control (P4) this yields 180 runs; one run of the main configuration produces both the RCS-included and RCS-excluded arms. The UCB1 sweep in Section 9.2 adds a further 90.

sections.heading: Held-out RCS reporting.
sections.text: Internal logs contain clipped summary fields (Appendix A ); all tables and figures report the raw, unclipped post-hoc estimator output ( uncapped ), though the estimator’s per-drop rules still apply (Section 9.4 ). Held-out RCS enters neither the objective nor winner selection, so it cannot leak test information into search.

The null is informative not because these tests found nothing, but because instructed minimization reaches a level below the mean claim volume at every pressure level on the four datasets where it reduced claims ( 18 18 – 35 % 35\% below default, Section 9.3 ; × \times in Figure 2 a) — three of those reductions ( 27 27 – 35 % 35\% ) being 2.4 2.4 – 3.1 × 3.1\times the replicate band of Section 8 and Credit-G’s 18 % 18\% only 1.6 × 1.6\times . Under Equation 3 , deleting one inert claim at λ nom = 20 \lambda_{\mathrm{nom}}=20 would raise the objective by ρ / ( | E P | − 1 ) \rho/(|E_{P}|-1) accuracy standard deviations ( ≈ 1.2 \approx 1.2 on Credit-G, ≈ 2.1 \approx 2.1 on Madelon; Table 7 ). This is an upper bound, since joint interventions can absorb a deletion; a direct claim-deletion test with the pipeline held fixed is future work. Held-out fidelity moves independently of claim volume. On Credit-G, uncapped held-out RCS falls from 0.053 0.053 at λ nom = 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{nom}}=0 to 0.022 0.022 at λ nom = 5 \lambda_{\mathrm{nom}}=5 while claim counts stay flat, then partly recovers to 0.044 0.044 at λ nom = 20 \lambda_{\mathrm{nom}}=20 . The CIs overlap and the × 0.42 \times 0.42 excursion is only marginally outside the replicate band, so it suggests fidelity moving with flat counts, not pressure-induced drift.

sections.heading: 9.3 Capability control: minimization is possible when instructed
sections.text: At λ nom = 5 \lambda_{\mathrm{nom}}=5 (Table 5 , Figure 3 ; Appendix C ), the minimize prompt reduces claim volume on four of six datasets: Butterfly − 35 % -35\% , Electricity − 34 % -34\% , Madelon − 27 % -27\% , Credit-G − 18 % -18\% — three of five without Butterfly; the other two change little (Ecommerce − 0.0 % -0.0\% , Breast − 1.7 % -1.7\% ), so the control is inconclusive there. Held-out RCS rises or falls (Credit-G × 0.60 \times 0.60 , Butterfly × 0.79 \times 0.79 , Madelon × 1.77 \times 1.77 ) within or at the edge of the replicate band, so this arm bears on volume only. The contrast with Section 9.2 is our central result: shorter claim lists are reachable, but search — Thompson sampling or UCB1 — did not find them without instruction. Given feedback without claim counts and ≤ 38 \leq 38 proposals, this null is largely structural; the control shows only reachability.

sections.heading: 9.4 Probe access produces selection (F4)
sections.text: Table 6 and Figure 4 (both Appendix C ) compare agents that differ only in access to probe_feature_drop , which the probe arm calls 3.1 3.1 – 3.9 3.9 times per iteration against a budget of four. The selection signature stated in Section 6.3 — claim volume falls while verified-claim rate rises — appears on Butterfly (claims 15.5 → 14.3 15.5\to 14.3 , verified rate 0.49 → 0.50 0.49\to 0.50 ), Madelon ( 25.6 → 14.8 25.6\to 14.8 , 0.50 → 0.51 0.50\to 0.51 ), Credit-G ( 12.4 → 11.7 12.4\to 11.7 , 0.40 → 0.50 0.40\to 0.50 ), and Breast ( 10.5 → 10.3 10.5\to 10.3 , 0.38 → 0.41 0.38\to 0.41 ) — three of five without Butterfly. The remaining two do not exhibit it: Ecommerce’s verified rate also falls ( 0.54 → 0.49 0.54\to 0.49 ) and Electricity’s claim volume rises ( 8.9 → 11.1 8.9\to 11.1 ). Only Madelon’s volume drop ( − 42 % -42\% ) and Credit-G’s rate rise ( + 0.10 +0.10 ) exceed the replicate band. On Credit-G, held-out fidelity drops with non-overlapping CIs ( 0.034 0.034 to 0.016 0.016 ); on Ecommerce and Madelon the point estimates fall by half or more ( 0.069 → 0.024 0.069\to 0.024 , 0.188 → 0.095 0.188\to 0.095 ) but with large seed spread. All three ratios ( × 0.46 \times 0.46 , × 0.35 \times 0.35 , × 0.50 \times 0.50 ) fall below the replicate band’s lower end ( × 0.61 \times 0.61 ); reporting only the verified-claim rate would record improvement as fidelity degrades. Scoring is asymmetric: all Credit-G and two Madelon probe-access winners use ≤ 10 \leq 10 features, and the estimator’s small-pipeline rules (Appendix A ) apply only to them, so part of those declines may be scoring artifacts; Ecommerce ( 40 40 – 76 76 features) is unaffected but has overlapping CIs.

sections.heading: Scope and power.
sections.text: One verifier of our own, one generator model (Solar Pro 3), six datasets, and pipeline-design tasks with mechanical counterfactuals make the evidence preliminary. Butterfly, our sole image task, reaches only ≈ 0.19 \approx 0.19 accuracy, so counts are also reported without it. Our per-dataset trend tests detect only large effects (Section 9.2 ), so we report the absence of discovered claim-gaming, not equivalence; pooling datasets in a mixed model is future work.

sections.heading: Generator variation and unswept settings.
sections.text: Decoding parameters were fixed, but the hosted generator’s served checkpoint cannot be identified. The replicate band of Section 8 rests on one pair of runs, so it is an order of magnitude for fixed-seed noise, not an interval, and verdicts near its edges may change with more replicates. Estimator constants (Appendix A ) were not swept.

sections.heading: Normalization and untested channels.
sections.text: ρ \rho can inflate on low-variance tasks without changing selection, so we report decision impact separately (Table 4 ). We did not test rephrasing that lowers the parsed claim count, search that observes claim count (the most direct probe of F3), and delayed or committed oracle access; our four-call probe channel is noiseless and immediate.

sections.heading: 11 Conclusion
sections.text: We propose a stress-test methodology for an agent’s own verifier — the pressure ratio ρ \rho , four falsifiable probes, and a reporting standard — that needs only an optimizing loop around a scalar verifier; its extension to tests, task completion, or citation grounding is a hypothesis. Across six datasets and 180 runs (plus a 90-run sweep) with one verifier and one generator, search did not discover claim minimization even at ρ \rho over two orders above deployment , although instructed agents stated fewer claims — a null that is largely structural. In summary: report ρ \rho , count claims separately from scores, pair F3 robustness claims with a capability control, and measure fidelity on verifier-unseen data.

sections.heading: Verification-aware final selection.
sections.text: Beyond the objective term, the deployed system consults the verifier once more when it selects the pipeline to report: among candidates whose validation accuracy lies within a per-dataset tolerance ( 0.004 0.004 – 0.02 0.02 , expanded to 0.035 0.035 for Credit-G) of the best, it prefers the one with the higher verification RCS — ordered by its real-signal, tested-claim, and nonzero-drop counts — before falling back to reward and feature compactness. This tie-break is enabled in the deployed dynamic- λ \lambda configuration on all six datasets. It is a further channel through which the verifier shapes the reported artifact but which ρ \rho does not register, since ρ \rho (Equation 4 ) measures only the objective term; we disclose it so that the verifier’s full influence is on record. Held-out RCS (Section 8 ) remains a post-hoc diagnostic and enters neither the objective nor this tie-break.

sections.heading: Joint interventions.
sections.text: When three or more feature-importance claims are stated (two or more for low-accuracy image runs, where validation accuracy is below 0.10 0.10 ), a subset of the named features (one if at most ten features are selected, otherwise up to half) is removed together in a single counterfactual and the one resulting drop is used, rather than removing each feature separately.
